strengths: Comprehensive and well-structured evaluation spanning academic benchmarks (SCROLLS, multi-hop QA), real-world applications (user behavior QA, a 128k-token agent task on Terminal-Bench), and extreme-length synthetic retrieval (1M tokens), with a consistent ~3k memory budget across baselines.

CoMeT achieves the best average score among efficient plug-and-play methods on SCROLLS and matches the fine-tuned full-attention baseline on summarization tasks using only ~2.5k memory tokens, which is a meaningful result for the constant-memory regime.

The dual-memory design (gated global state + FIFO temporary memory) is clearly motivated, and the ablations directly support each design choice: temporary memory drives in-domain performance, global memory drives length extrapolation, and removing the gate causes complete collapse (Figure 8).

The gating-value visualization over all 36 layers (Figures 10, 11) provides genuinely interesting interpretability evidence that gates open at the passkey location and then shield the stored information, corroborating the mechanistic claims.

The layer-level pipeline parallelism strategy is a practical contribution (2.7x speedup over naive context parallelism, 128k fine-tuning on 16x80GB GPUs), and training/efficiency analysis (prefill/decode latency, constant ~10GB memory) is thorough and includes both large and small models.

Reproducibility support is above average for this area: full training hyperparameters, baseline configurations, chunk/compression-token configurations, and passkey prompt format are provided, and code is stated to be released.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental relative to the recurrent-memory line the paper itself surveys: memory tokens with chunk recurrence (Memformer, RMT), a dual-queue recent/compressed memory (Compressive Transformer), and hierarchical memory with gating (HMT, ARMT). The specific combination plus the LSTM-style gate is well-executed but the conceptual delta over HMT in particular is not sharply articulated beyond 'we add a gate and a FIFO queue'.

All headline results appear to come from single runs; no seeds, standard deviations, or significance tests are reported, despite several close comparisons (e.g., CoMeT avg 40.10 vs. SWA 38.24; GovRep metrics within ~1-2 points of Full Attn FT).

The 1M-token passkey result is impressive but the model is fine-tuned directly on the passkey task at 32k; extrapolation claims rest on a synthetic task, and no out-of-distribution real data (e.g., natural text) is evaluated at >32k lengths, so the extrapolation generality is unverified.

Two of the three real-world evaluations use proprietary or expert-curated datasets (e-commerce UQA, custom agent trajectories), limiting independent reproducibility of the practical-utility claims; the UQA comparison also mixes a 4k CoMeT vs. a 32k Full Attn upper bound with LLM-as-judge scoring using a same-family (Qwen) judge model.

Baseline coverage in the finite-state category is thin: RMT, ARMT, and other recurrent memory transformers are discussed at length in Related Work but not compared, and stronger modern baselines (e.g., gated linear attention hybrids, Infinity/infini-attention style methods) are absent; the pipeline-parallelism speedup is only measured against the authors' naive strawman rather than an established context-parallelism baseline.

Some methodological details are underspecified: how the LM loss is scoped (chunk tokens only vs. all tokens), the effect of chunk size (2048) on results, and why Full Attn (FT) scores on Qasper (40.3 F1) are low relative to typical reported numbers for this benchmark, raising questions about the mixed-training setup used for all baselines.

Several claims are overstated relative to evidence: 'the limits of information theory' framing for compression methods is rhetorical rather than argued, and 'pushing the boundaries of what is possible' language is not matched by comparisons showing feasibility gaps versus prior recurrent approaches.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning SCROLLS, shorter-context QA, real-world user-behavior QA and agent tasks, plus synthetic passkey retrieval, giving a broad picture of the method's operating envelope.
CoMeT achieves the best average score among efficient methods on SCROLLS (40.10) under a comparable ~3k memory budget, and matches the fine-tuned full-attention baseline on summarization tasks.

Well-designed ablations that cleanly disentangle the roles of the two memory components: temporary memory drives in-domain performance (Figure 7) while the gated global memory drives length extrapolation (Figure 8), and the no-gate collapse directly supports the gating design choice.

Thorough efficiency analysis with prefill/decode latency and memory measurements up to 1M tokens, and a practical layer-level pipeline parallelism strategy with a reported 2.7x speedup over naive context parallelism.

The gating-value visualization (Figure 10) provides interpretable evidence that the learned gate opens at the passkey chunk and then shields the stored information, going beyond black-box benchmark numbers.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the architecture is a fairly direct combination of existing ideas — chunk recurrence with memory tokens (RMT, Memformer, HMT), a FIFO of compressed recent states (Compressive Transformer), and an LSTM-style gated state update. The delta over the closest prior work (HMT) is not clearly articulated or empirically isolated beyond adding the gate.

Reproducibility concerns: the code URL is left empty in the manuscript, the UQA dataset is proprietary and cannot be released, and the agent dataset is only loosely described ('expert-driven methodology'), so the headline real-world claims cannot be independently verified.

The models are fine-tuned on data drawn from the very SCROLLS tasks used for evaluation, which weakens claims of general long-context capability; while baselines receive the same treatment, the paper does not report any held-out-task or out-of-domain generalization results for the academic benchmarks.

Some reported gains are modest or unconvincing: on Terminal-Bench, CoMeT (20.27) actually underperforms full attention (21.33); the SCROLLS advantage over the strong fine-tuned SWA baseline is ~1.9 points with no variance, significance testing, or multiple seeds; Activation Beacon's anomalously low CNLI score (25.8) is not discussed.

The striking 1M-token extrapolation claim rests solely on a synthetic passkey task on which the model was specifically fine-tuned; no evidence is provided that complex reasoning or language understanding survives at such lengths, yet the abstract and conclusion generalize to 'arbitrarily long' context handling.

The headline 21x/10x efficiency figures (Figures 1b, 1c) are measured on a tiny 768-dimensional, 12-layer model rather than the 4B model used for quality results, which somewhat undermines their practical relevance.

Several methodological details that affect the comparison are under-justified, e.g., CoMeT uses a smaller memory budget (2560) than baselines (~3072) 'as demonstrated in Table 7', but Table 7 only shows SCROLLS-average scaling curves, not the per-method fairness argument.

strengths: Strong empirical results: CoMeT achieves the best average score among efficient methods on SCROLLS (40.10 vs. 38.24 for the next best, SWA), matches the fine-tuned full-attention baseline on summarization tasks (GovRep, SummScr) with only ~2.5k memory tokens, and matches full attention on short-context QA.

Impressive length extrapolation: trained only on 32k contexts, the model perfectly solves the passkey task at 1M tokens, supported by clear ablations (Figure 8) showing that the gated global memory—not temporary memory—is the critical component for extrapolation, and that removing the gate causes complete collapse.

The gated state update (Eq. 2) with the low-rank RLA transformation is a sensible, parameter-efficient design, and the analysis (Figure 7, Figure 10 gating-value visualization showing gate values dropping to 0 at the passkey chunk and closing afterward) provides genuine mechanistic insight rather than just benchmark numbers.
The layer-level pipeline parallelism strategy is a practical contribution, enabling 128k-token fine-tuning on 16×80GB GPUs with a reported 2.7× speedup over naive context parallelism.

Evaluation spans synthetic (passkey), academic (SCROLLS, 2WikiMQA/HotpotQA), and real-world (UQA, Terminal-Bench) settings, and efficiency is analyzed separately for prefill and decode phases with asymptotic behavior validated on a smaller model.
The paper is clearly written, with a useful notation table, detailed experimental setup (Appendix A), and publicly released code.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the design is a synthesis of well-known ingredients—memory tokens (RMT, Memformer), compressed memory queues (Compressive Transformer), sensory/summarization memories (HMT)—with an LSTM-style gate. The paper's positioning against HMT, its closest competitor, rests largely on the gating mechanism; a more direct head-to-head ablation isolating this difference on the same memory budget would strengthen the case (the Figure 8d gate ablation helps but is only on the synthetic task).

Baseline fairness is not fully convincing: training-free compression methods are evaluated on the fine-tuned full-attention model while fine-tunable baselines are fine-tuned separately, and several baselines (e.g., HMT at 30.31, Activation Beacon's 25.8 on CNLI) appear substantially below published figures, raising the possibility of under-tuned comparisons.

CoMeT does not actually match full attention overall on SCROLLS (40.10 vs. 42.23); it trails notably on Qasper (35.5 vs. 40.3) and ContractNLI (86.9 vs. 89.1). The headline claim is carefully scoped to summarization, but the abstract's framing ('surpasses other efficient methods... performance comparable to full attention') could overstate the result.

Reproducibility gaps for the real-world claims: the UQA dataset is proprietary and anonymous with LLM-as-judge evaluation, and the Long-Horizon Agent dataset's construction is described only at a high level. Terminal-Bench results (20.27 vs. 21.33 full attention) use configurations that no baseline could be trained under, so this comparison is not fully controlled.

The information-theoretic argument against compression methods (compressed length 'must inevitably grow' with the original) is asserted rather than substantiated, and the claim that such methods cannot be trained at 128k (precluding baselines on the agent task) is asserted without evidence—HMT-style methods plausibly could be.
Single-run results with no variance estimates or significance testing; differences between CoMeT and the strongest baselines on some datasets (e.g., Qspr) are within plausible noise.

Missing comparison to some closely related recurrent approaches cited in related work (e.g., Infini-attention, which is used as the passkey task source, and ARMT), and the 1M-token capability is demonstrated only on the synthetic passkey task; no real comprehension benchmark is evaluated at extrapolated lengths.

strengths: Comprehensive and well-designed evaluation: SCROLLS with a broad set of compression and finite-state baselines under a unified memory budget (~3k tokens), shorter-context QA (2WikiMQA/HotpotQA), long-context extrapolation subset, a 1M-token passkey task, and two application scenarios (UQA, Terminal-Bench), covering both effectiveness and efficiency (latency/VRAM scaling).

The central claims are supported by the evidence: constant memory and linear-time behavior is demonstrated empirically (Figures 1, 9, Table 8, including a comparison with RWKV-7), and 32k->1M extrapolation on passkey retrieval is convincingly shown.

Thorough ablations isolate the roles of the two memories (Figure 7, Figure 8), the gating mechanism (its removal causes collapse), RLA rank (Table 6), and hyperparameters (Table 9); the gate-value visualization (Figures 10, 12) provides mechanistic insight into how the global state protects salient information.
Generalization across model families and scales (Qwen3-4B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B) with a small parameter overhead (0.098%) supports the plug-and-play claim.
The layer-level pipeline parallelism is a practical systems contribution (2.7x speedup over naive context parallelism) enabling 128k fine-tuning on 16x80GB GPUs, and it is clearly illustrated.
The paper is clearly written, includes a limitations section, an honest failure-case analysis (Appendix J), and releases code, supporting reproducibility on the public benchmarks.
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is incremental: gated global state + FIFO 'recent' memory closely mirrors the Compressive Transformer's dual-queue design and RMT-style memory tokens; the main new elements are the RLA low-rank state-to-memory projection, the scalar gate, and the pipeline-parallelism scheme. The paper would benefit from a sharper articulation of what is fundamentally new over Compressive Transformer/RMT/ARMT.

The argument that context-compression methods are 'constrained by information theory' and only improve constant factors is overstated as a motivation; compression methods were never claimed to change asymptotic complexity, and this framing sets up a somewhat strawman comparison.

Reproducibility gaps: the UQA dataset is proprietary e-commerce data and cannot be reproduced or compared by others; the long-horizon agent dataset construction is described only at a high level; Terminal-Bench results use an 8B backbone and a setup (128k trajectories) under which other efficient methods were not trained, so that comparison is asymmetric and not fully controlled.

The Llama-3.1 result where CoMeT surpasses fine-tuned full attention by 4.6% is surprising; the paper does not investigate whether the full-attention baseline was under-tuned, which would strengthen confidence in the baseline comparisons.

Position-handling details (e.g., how positional encodings/rope are treated across chunks) and the exact treatment of readout/compression token supervision are under-specified in the main text, which matters for reproducing extrapolation behavior.

Passkey retrieval is a synthetic, single-fact task; extrapolation claims would be more convincing with longer real-data extrapolation beyond the 91k-average SCROLLS subset (where CoMeT still trails full attention), and with deeper analysis of whether the gating has learned a shortcut for the synthetic task format.

strengths: The paper is empirically thorough for an architecture/systems paper: SCROLLS plus QA benchmarks, three backbone models (Qwen3-4B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B) testing generality, ablations over memory allocation, RLA rank, chunk size, and gating, an efficiency analysis of prefill/decode latency and memory, and a qualitative failure-case analysis.
The gating visualization (Figures 8, 10, 12) provides mechanistic evidence supporting the central claim that the gated update protects long-term information, going beyond purely end-task metrics.

The layer-level pipeline parallelism strategy is a concrete, useful engineering contribution (2.7x speedup over naive context parallelism) that makes 128k-context training feasible on modest hardware.
The method is genuinely parameter-efficient (~4M added parameters) and the code is released, supporting reproducibility of the main pipeline.
The honesty of some negative results (e.g., CoMeT does not match full attention on the >32k SCROLLS subset, Table 7) increases trust in the reported gains.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: chunk-recurrent memory tokens with a gated state update closely recombines well-known ideas (RMT/Memformer memory tokens, Compressive Transformer dual queues, LSTM-style gating, Infini-attention's local+compressive-memory design). The paper does not clearly articulate a conceptual advance beyond assembling these components, and comparisons to the closest method (Infini-attention) are absent.

The headline 1M-token extrapolation result is only on the synthetic passkey task, a weak proxy for long-context understanding; on realistic >32k SCROLLS data CoMeT falls well short of full attention (e.g., NrtvQA 13.2 vs 20.4), and the paper attributes the gap partly to the backbone's native 256k context rather than to the method's limits.

Several claims are overstated relative to the evidence: 'on par' with fine-tuned full attention on summarization (40.10 vs 42.23 average) is not on par; 'minimal fine-tuning' actually involves 3 epochs on a 32k mixed corpus; and CoMeT exceeding the full-attention 'upper bound' by 4.6% on Llama suggests the upper-bound baseline itself is unstable or under-tuned, which undermines the comparison framing.

The SCROLLS fine-tuned baseline numbers appear low relative to published results for comparable models, raising concerns about the unified training configuration and whether all baselines were given equally careful tuning.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the UQA benchmark is proprietary (real-world e-commerce logs) with an LLM-as-judge protocol, and the agent dataset construction and Terminal-Bench setup lack sufficient detail for independent replication.
No variance estimates, seeds, or significance tests are reported for any comparison, despite differences among efficient methods often being small (e.g., CoMeT 40.10 vs SWA 38.24).
The information-theoretic argument against compression methods (citing Shannon, 1948) is hand-wavy and does not rigorously establish the claimed asymptotic distinction.

Inference is inherently sequential chunk-by-chunk, limiting prefill parallelism in deployment; the efficiency analysis reports wall-clock results but does not discuss this structural limitation or compare against parallelizable recurrent baselines beyond RWKV7 at short lengths.

strengths: Comprehensive and well-designed empirical evaluation spanning synthetic (passkey), academic (SCROLLS, 2WikiMQA/HotpotQA), and real-world (UQA, Terminal-Bench) settings, with a fair ~3k-token memory budget imposed on all efficient baselines.

The headline result is striking and well-supported: a module trained only on 32k contexts retrieves passkeys at any depth up to 1M tokens with constant memory and linear time, backed by latency/VRAM measurements (Figures 1, 9, Table 8) and an RWKV-7 comparison.

Thorough ablations: memory allocation (Figure 7), gating removal causing collapse (Figure 8d), RLA rank sensitivity (Table 6), chunk size/stride (Table 9), and gating-value visualizations that provide mechanistic insight into how the gate preserves passkey information.
Generalization is tested across three model families and two scales (Table 5), strengthening the plug-and-play claim beyond a single backbone.
The layer-level pipeline parallelism contribution is practically useful (2.7x speedup) and clearly explained with bubble visualizations.
Good reproducibility overall: training configurations, baseline configurations, dataset construction, and prompts are documented in appendices, and code is released.
weaknesses: Architectural novelty is incremental: gated additive state updates (LSTM/GRU-style), memory tokens with readout (RMT/Memformer), FIFO secondary memory (Compressive Transformer), and compression tokens (AutoCompressor/ICAE) are all established; the contribution is primarily a careful combination and engineering, which limits the conceptual advance.

Missing comparisons with the most closely related recurrent-memory methods: Infini-attention (the very work whose passkey setup is adopted), ARMT, and HMT appear in related work or baselines, but ARMT and Infini-attention are not empirically compared, weakening claims of superiority among finite-state approaches.

Extrapolation evidence rests heavily on a synthetic passkey task; the real-data extrapolation subset (Table 7) shows CoMeT still trails full attention substantially on >32k inputs, so the 1M-token claim's practical significance is narrower than the abstract implies.

The surprising result that CoMeT beats fine-tuned full attention by 4.6% on Llama-3.1-8B (Table 5) is not analyzed or explained, raising questions about evaluation noise or baseline tuning; no variance, seeds, or significance testing is reported anywhere.

The UQA benchmark uses proprietary e-commerce data with LLM-as-judge evaluation (Qwen2.5-72B), which is neither reproducible nor verifiable; the 2.7-point margin over xRAG cannot be independently checked.

Inference costs are not fully accounted for: decode is constant at ~22ms per token regardless of context, but prefill is strictly sequential and chunk-by-chunk (95s at 1M), and the paper does not discuss throughput implications for streaming vs. one-shot use, or whether global memory single-vector states across layers create information bottlenecks beyond what ablations show.

The pipeline parallelism scheme, while effective, is a fairly straightforward fine-grained pipelining of the inherent serial dependency; its novelty relative to standard micro-batched pipeline parallelism deserves more careful differentiation.
Claimed 21x/10x speedup and memory figures are against a full-attention baseline that OOMs at 128k under their setup, so the ratios depend on the specific hardware and serving configuration.
